supporting_evidence_json: Scope s05 requires explanations, responsibility maps, and architecture reviews built from repository analysis.
s04 ties views to a selected saved scan and query. It rejects outdated browser replies and does not guarantee that every runtime relationship is found.
The product (s01) requires every result to keep its evidence, its uncertainty, whether its inputs are still current, and a note on anything shortened.
Proposal B lists confirming the claim-book fit with parents f0c461 and 877208 as an unknown.
Proposal C states that failing to read the selected analysis prevents all outputs.
Proposal A admits that separate requests may rebuild the same map.

assessments.change_isolation: A new review rule only changes the review function. A new grouping rule changes the map, and through it every explanation and review that uses the map. New output formats go in the parent.
assessments.control_flow: The parent calls one function per request. Explanation and review call the map function when they need it. There is no runner, queue, or controller.
assessments.data_ownership: The parent keeps scans, settings, progress, and saved outputs. The functions keep only temporary working values. Each answer names its scan, query, and settings.
assessments.decomposition: The work is split by output type: map, explanation, and review. Reading the evidence is not a separate step. Each function reads the selected analysis on its own.
assessments.failure_isolation: Each output succeeds or fails on its own. If the map fails, an explanation or review can still return the parts it can support and mark itself incomplete. Crash protection belongs to the parent.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all three required outputs. It keeps evidence links and uncertainty, and it says when information is missing. The evidence and uncertainty rules for shortened answers are stated directly.
assessments.justified_complexity: This is the smallest design: three functions and two calls between them. It adds a saved map only if measured repeated work justifies it. That is a reasonable way to delay complexity.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside whatever execution the parent already uses. That includes bounded worker processes, meaning separate processes with fixed limits. It gives no protection from crashes; that protection depends on the parent.
strengths: Each output (map, explanation, review) has one function, and that function owns the answer.
Explanations and reviews call the same map function, so a review judges the same groups a reader sees in the map.
It saves nothing itself, so it fits all three parent designs without taking over any of their saved data.
A free-form reader question goes straight to the explanation function, so questions the map does not cover can still get an answer.
weaknesses: Separate requests can rebuild the same map again and again. The proposal admits this.
If the grouping logic puts a file in the wrong group, that mistake shows up in maps, explanations, and reviews alike.
The parent must handle saving, cancellation, freshness checks, and old browser replies. Most of the coordination work moves to the parent.
Nothing guarantees that an explanation and a map built at different times use the same grouping settings, unless the parent records those settings.

assessments.change_isolation: New output kinds and new grouping methods are added without touching old claims. New review rules need a new method version and sometimes new kinds of claims.
assessments.control_flow: A build request picks a scan, groups and saves the claims, then judges and saves the judgments. A read request picks a scan, reads the claims, adds a freshness note, builds the output, and tags the reply. A read never starts a build by itself.
assessments.data_ownership: This capability owns the claim book. Claims are only added, and they are filed by scan and method version. Only the claim checker may add them. s04 keeps the scans. Outputs are not saved.
assessments.decomposition: The work is split by step: pick the scan, group, check, save, judge the design, build the output, check for a newer scan, and drop old replies. The three outputs are only different views of the saved claims.
assessments.failure_isolation: A failed run adds a 'stopped early' marker, and the claims already saved stay readable. A claim with a broken evidence link is rejected alone. A failed output build loses nothing. A claim-book failure affects every repository.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all three outputs. It traces evidence most strongly of the three. It fits fixed maps and reviews better than open reader questions.
assessments.justified_complexity: It has eight parts and a permanent store. That cost buys traceability and history, which the product does ask for. But the scope does not require keeping a history of interpretations, so part of the cost answers a need the scope never states.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the same installed application as s04. Its permanent store must fit the parent's rules for writing saved data, and how long to keep data is unknown.
strengths: All three outputs are rebuilt from the same saved claims, so they cannot contradict each other.
Every review judgment must point to claims, and every claim must point to scan evidence. That chain lets a reader check why a statement was made.

Claims are only added, never edited, and each one is tagged with its scan and grouping-method version. Readers can compare what was said about an old scan with what is said about a new one. This partly addresses s04's open question about telling newer interpretations apart.
Building claims and reading output are separate requests, so a slow build never blocks reading older results.
When two claims disagree, both are kept and the disagreement is marked, instead of one being picked quietly.
weaknesses: It creates its own permanent store, the claim book. Parent f0c461 lets only its request gate write saved data. Parent 877208 lets only its controller accept results. The proposal says this fit is unconfirmed.
Explanations are built only from saved claims. A reader question that no claim covers may get no answer, or only 'not built yet'.
A new review rule may first need new kinds of claims, which slows changes.
Old claim sets pile up until a cleanup step exists, and no cleanup step is defined.
Rebuilding output on every read repeats work. Adding a cache would bring back the risk of stale copies.
If the claim book fails, new builds stop for every repository. The proposal admits it does not isolate this.

assessments.change_isolation: A new review rule changes only the writer. A new output type needs a builder only if it needs its own failure state. A change to evidence reading affects all outputs.
assessments.control_flow: One runner controls the order of steps and checks for cancellation between steps. If one output fails, the other independent outputs still run. The collector marks unfinished outputs.
assessments.data_ownership: The parent keeps scans, access decisions, progress, and saved results. The runner keeps temporary step states. The collector holds the result until the parent takes it.
assessments.decomposition: The work is split by step within one request: read the evidence, build the map, write, and collect the result. The explanation and review writers are combined into one part.
assessments.failure_isolation: Map, explanation, and review failures are recorded separately. A failure to read the evidence stops everything. Crashes lose unsaved work unless the parent prevents it.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all three outputs. It says when a review is weaker because no map was available. It keeps observed facts, inferred groups, and suggested changes apart.
assessments.justified_complexity: It adds a runner and a result collector on top of A's parts. That extra cost buys one shared evidence read and one combined result for each request. It stays small, with no queue and no store.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the parent's existing execution. Under parent 877208, the proposal admits its sequence of steps may need splitting to fit worker limits.
strengths: It reads the evidence once per request, so all outputs in that request use the same selected analysis.
Each output gets its own completion state, and a failed review does not erase a finished map.
Saving belongs to the parent, so there is no second store and no second controller.
Saving the settings used with each output helps readers see why two reviews differ.
weaknesses: If reading the analysis fails, every output fails. The shared evidence step is one point of failure.
Outputs are built one after another, which can slow responses.
A crash before the parent saves can lose outputs that were already finished.
Explanation and review share one writer part, so a change to how reviews are written also touches explanation writing.
The map is reused only within one request. Separate requests still rebuild it.

composition_conflicts: B's claim checker must be the only writer to the claim book. Parent f0c461 lets only its request gate write saved data, so two parts would each claim sole write rights.
Parent 877208 lets only its controller accept findings and change saved progress. B's claim book would need to go through that controller. The proposal leaves this unconfirmed.
If A's or C's map is combined with B, map results must be saved as checked claims. Otherwise maps and reviews could drift apart.
C's sequence of steps may exceed the limits of parent 877208's bounded workers, meaning separate processes with fixed limits. The steps may then need splitting.
disagreements: A and C say outputs need no store of their own. B says permanent claims are needed for agreement between outputs and for history.
A lets each output read the analysis on its own. C says one shared evidence read per request keeps outputs tied to the same analysis.
B refuses to start a build during a read and returns 'not built yet'. A and C always calculate the answer when asked.

differences: B keeps its own permanent claim store. In A and C, the parent keeps all saved data.
A starts one separate call per output. C runs one request that builds several outputs in order and returns them together.
C reads the evidence once and shares it with every output in the request. A reads the analysis inside each function. B reads it once per build and saves the claims.
B rebuilds outputs from saved claims on every read. A and C write each output fresh from the analysis.
Where a failure spreads differs. In C, a failed evidence read stops every output. In B, a failed claim book stops all builds for every repository. In A, each output fails alone.
limitations: A and C both keep no saved data, rely on the parent for saving, and share the map within a request. They mostly differ in who sets the order of steps.
All three are paper designs. Grouping quality, review quality, and speed are unproven.
unexplored_directions: Saving a map in the parent, keyed by scan and settings, so separate requests can reuse it.
Letting readers or agents correct a wrong responsibility group and feed that fix back into later outputs.
Sending partial results to readers before a long build finishes.
Reusing groups from an older scan and updating only the parts that changed.
Answering open reader questions from saved claims and falling back to direct analysis when no claim covers them.

evidence: Scope s05 requires explanations, responsibility maps, and architecture reviews built from repository analysis.
s04 ties views to a selected saved scan and query. It rejects outdated browser replies and does not guarantee that every runtime relationship is found.
The product (s01) requires every result to keep its evidence, its uncertainty, whether its inputs are still current, and a note on anything shortened.
Proposal B lists confirming the claim-book fit with parents f0c461 and 877208 as an unknown.
Proposal C states that failing to read the selected analysis prevents all outputs.
Proposal A admits that separate requests may rebuild the same map.
value_json.summary: All three proposals produce explanations, responsibility maps, and architecture reviews from a saved scan picked out by s04. They differ in who keeps results and how the work is split. A gives each output its own function and saves nothing. C runs one request that reads the evidence once, builds the outputs in order, and hands back one combined result. C also saves nothing. B saves every statement as a permanent claim in its own claim book. B then rebuilds each output from those claims whenever someone reads it. A and C are fairly close: in both, the parent application keeps all saved data. B is the only one that keeps its own saved data, and that clashes with two of the three parent designs. None of the three is declared the winner.
unknowns: None of the proposals defines the review criteria or the format of evidence references.
No proposal says how good the responsibility groups must be or how to measure that.
How s04 historical views tell newer interpretations apart is still undefined.
Maximum answer sizes and how to shorten answers in practice are unspecified.
Whether review judgments come from fixed rules, model workers, or people is not given.

value_json.summary: The assessment holds up against the supplied source. In config.py, _architecture_config, _agent_config and load_config call .get or .items on YAML sections without first checking that each section is a mapping (a dictionary of named settings). supporting_evidence_json: Scope s02 says graph findings do not automatically authorize deletion or refactoring.
Scope s04 ties graph pages to a saved scan and query and does not guarantee finding every relationship that appears while the program runs.
Scope s01 requires that results keep evidence, uncertainty, and whether their inputs are still current, and that shortened results disclose what they left out.
B's own parent notes say that with f0c461 the request gate does the assessment write, and that it assumes stable IDs from s04.
A's parent notes say that parent 877208 runs on permitted captured findings.

assessments.change_isolation: Strong. Pattern logic and edit logic live in separate actions. Only the reader is shared. A new output format goes in the parent, so the assessment rules stay unchanged.
assessments.control_flow: The parent calls one action directly. That action reads evidence, reasons, and returns. Each request is handled by a single call, and there are no steps in between.
assessments.data_ownership: The exploration capability (s04) owns scans and findings. The parent owns saved assessments and access settings. Each action keeps only temporary working data. The reader keeps no copies.
assessments.decomposition: The split follows the two kinds of question users ask, plus one reader for evidence. There is no coordinator.
assessments.failure_isolation: A failure in one action does not cancel the other action's finished result. Missing evidence produces an incomplete result or a stated uncertainty. A crash of the whole program is not contained. That depends on the parent.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers both required judgments and keeps each one tied to its evidence and its chosen scan. Its fit is weaker when one request needs both judgments or a combined answer.
assessments.justified_complexity: Low complexity, and the required functions justify it. Nothing is added that the scope does not ask for.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the parent. It depends on the parent for access checks, cancellation, saving, shortening results, and error codes. It fits all three parent designs.
strengths: It is the smallest design. It has three parts: one finding reader and two judgment actions. It adds no service and no saved data of its own.
Pattern advice and edit advice can change separately, because neither action calls the other.
One shared reader handles missing evidence the same way for both actions. It never switches quietly to a newer scan.
weaknesses: Each action carries its own copy of the rule that a finding is not permission to delete or refactor. Nothing checks the final wording in one place, so the two copies can drift apart.
A request for both judgments runs two separate actions. They may repeat work or disagree, and nothing merges or compares the two answers.
It has no way to show later whether a past assessment is based on an outdated scan. That job is left entirely to the parent.
The shared reader is a single point of failure for both actions.

assessments.change_isolation: A new kind of judgment adds one drafting step. The steps that read findings, save records, and label freshness stay the same. But every wording rule lives in the limiter, so that one place can become hard to change.
assessments.control_flow: One fixed chain runs from start to end for each request. Nothing runs in the background. Re-showing a saved assessment skips the drafting step. If the request is interrupted, nothing is saved.
assessments.data_ownership: s04 owns findings. This scope owns only its never-edited assessment records, stored in the parent's store. Every other step keeps only data for the current request.
assessments.decomposition: The parts follow the order of the work: take the request, fetch findings, draft, limit the wording, save, label, and return.
assessments.failure_isolation: If the scan is missing, the request stops before drafting. A draft without evidence is turned down and not saved. A failed save leaves earlier records unchanged. If the newest scan cannot be found, the label says unknown. A program crash is not contained.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers both judgments and adds traceable records with freshness labels. The added freshness checking goes beyond the minimum requirement. It is useful only if s04 keeps old IDs stable.
assessments.justified_complexity: It is the most complex of the three, with seven parts and a saved record type. The limiter and the freshness label serve stated rules. The saved records serve a reuse need that the scope does not state.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the parent. With parent f0c461 it works only if that parent's request gate performs the assessment write. With parent 877208 the steps run inside a worker. That fits only if the worker may read s04 live, because that parent works from findings captured in advance.
strengths: One checker step, called the limiter, enforces the no-permission rule for every kind of assessment. It also turns down drafts that have no evidence or no notes on uncertainty.
Assessments point to findings by their ID and never copy them. So s04 stays the only keeper of findings, and copies cannot drift apart.
A freshness label is added each time a saved assessment is shown again. This directly meets the product rule that results must say whether their inputs are still current.
Saved assessments can be shown again later without redoing the judgment.
weaknesses: It assumes that s04 keeps stable IDs for old scans and findings, but the payload does not promise this. If s04 deletes or renumbers them, the saved citations stop working.
The label marks an assessment outdated whenever any newer scan exists, even if the cited findings did not change.
Records are added and never edited, so they pile up. No cleanup is defined.
Every read of s04 goes through one step. That step is a single point of failure and may slow down large requests.
It adds a saved record type to the parent's store. That gives this design more to carry than A or C.

assessments.change_isolation: Each new check states its question, the evidence it needs, and its possible outcomes. If one check depends on another, the request owner must declare that order, which limits hidden links between checks.
assessments.control_flow: The parent makes one call. The request owner reads the findings, picks checks, and runs them one by one. It records each outcome before starting the next check, then builds the report.
assessments.data_ownership: The request owner keeps the temporary status of each check. The reader keeps a copy of the evidence references for this request only. The parent owns saved records, attempts, and the browser's current selection.
assessments.decomposition: It has four parts: a request owner, a finding reader, a set of checks, and a report builder.
assessments.failure_isolation: An ordinary error in one check marks only that check as failed and keeps the earlier results. Missing essential findings stop the request with a stated reason. A program crash is not contained.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers both judgments as checks inside one request. It also gives the clearest account of partial and conflicting results.
assessments.justified_complexity: Moderate. The request owner and per-check status add parts, but they justify themselves by keeping partial results and showing what is missing. It adds no queue, retry loop, or saved progress.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs inside the parent and uses the parent's cancellation and resource limits. It fits all three parents. Under the worker parent, the controller accepts the output.
strengths: It tracks each small check as pending, running, complete, failed, unsupported, or interrupted. So a partial result can say exactly what is missing.
Conflicting conclusions stay visible in the report, each with its reasons, instead of one hiding the other.
One report builder words every deletion or refactoring idea as advice that needs a separate decision. So, like B's limiter, it enforces the no-permission rule in one place.
Cancellation stops new checks from starting and keeps the work already finished.
weaknesses: Checks run one after another, so broad assessments can be slow.
The status of each check exists only in memory. It is lost if the program crashes.
The parent's result formats have no defined place for the outcome of each check.
It does not specify how to choose which checks to run.

composition_conflicts: Under parent f0c461, only its request gate may write. B's records step writes on its own, so the gate must do that write for B to fit.
Parent 877208 runs workers on findings captured in advance. B fetches findings live and asks s04 for the newest scan, which may not be allowed inside a worker.
B cites findings by ID across time. s04 does not promise that old scans and IDs are kept stable.
C's per-check outcomes have no defined place in the parent's result formats, so shortening a result might drop them without saying so.
disagreements: B treats a stored, never-edited assessment record as part of this scope. A and C say saved records belong to the parent.
B blocks a draft that lacks evidence. A and C instead return the draft with the missing evidence marked as uncertain.
B says one request produces one draft from one drafting step. C says one request runs many checks and keeps conflicting answers side by side.

differences: Only B saves its own assessment records. A and C hand saving to the parent.
Only B checks freshness again each time a saved assessment is shown.
B and C each enforce the no-permission wording rule in one place. A repeats the rule inside each action.
C keeps the outcome of each check and combines them into one result. A returns two separate answers when both judgments are requested. B returns one draft from one drafting step.
limitations: A and C have nearly the same structure: one shared reader, judging parts that save nothing, and saving left to the parent. C mostly adds tracking of each check's status.
All three use one reader as the only way into s04, and all three run inside the parent's process.
None of the three contains a program crash or blocks late browser replies. All three pass both jobs to the parent.
unexplored_directions: Judging a proposed edit by comparing two saved scans, instead of reading one scan only.
Saving a frozen copy of the cited findings, so a citation still works if s04 deletes old scans.
Marking an assessment outdated only when the findings it cites change, not whenever any newer scan exists.
Requiring a recorded human decision before any assessment can feed an edit tool.
Running independent checks in parallel, with cancellation that works across them.

evidence: Scope s02 says graph findings do not automatically authorize deletion or refactoring.
Scope s04 ties graph pages to a saved scan and query and does not guarantee finding every relationship that appears while the program runs.
Scope s01 requires that results keep evidence, uncertainty, and whether their inputs are still current, and that shortened results disclose what they left out.
B's own parent notes say that with f0c461 the request gate does the assessment write, and that it assumes stable IDs from s04.
A's parent notes say that parent 877208 runs on permitted captured findings.
value_json.summary: All three designs judge coding patterns and proposed edits from findings in one chosen saved scan and query. All three never edit code. They differ in three ways. Design A gives the two kinds of judgment two separate entry points and saves nothing itself. Design B runs one fixed chain of steps. That chain has one checker that removes any approval wording, a store of records that are never edited, and a label that says whether a record's scan is still the newest one. Design C has one request owner that runs many small checks one after another, tracks how each check ended, and merges them into one report that can contain partial results. A and C are close: C is roughly A plus a step that tracks each check. All three run inside the parent program. All three rely on the parent to block crashes and to drop late browser replies.
unknowns: Which coding patterns and edit kinds must be assessed.
Whether s04 keeps old scans and their IDs indefinitely.
How s04 tells newer interpretations of old scans apart.
Whether assessments must be shown again later without redoing the judgment.
Any speed or size targets for assessments.

Workers pull items from the handout; nothing pushes work to them. Each worker answer goes to the result check, which records accepted or rejected. After each final item, the saved scan builder checks whether all items are final and, if so, seals the scan. A bad or late answer is rejected and recorded without affecting other items. Edits to the repository during a scan do not matter because work uses the snapshot. Unreadable files are listed in the snapshot rather than stopping it. A crash of the service loses no accepted work, because replaying the event list restores state, and the builder can run again with the same result. design.state_ownership: The event list owns all work state. The snapshot store owns frozen file text and hashes. The parent owns saved settings, access settings, and the store of sealed saved scans. The planner, structure reader, result check, and progress counter keep nothing between calls. Workers hold only the item they claimed until the time limit ends. No component keeps a second copy of progress.
design.summary: One record of work events is the only place where the state of a scan is kept. This record is a list of events that only grows: it is never edited, only added to. The design first takes a frozen copy of the repository's file contents, called a snapshot. Every later step works only from that copy. Planning work, checking worker answers, and building the final saved scan read from the snapshot and the event list. These steps keep nothing of their own. Progress is counted from the event list each time someone asks, so no separate counter can drift out of step. The final saved scan is built once from accepted results and is never changed after that. It is marked complete or incomplete, with a list of what is missing.
unknowns: The scope does not define the rules that decide whether work may start.

This means the repository's graph data can already be rebuilt from the git record. Event sourcing inside the tool would mostly add value for runtime job state, which git does not record.

value_json.summary: The assessment is sound. Event sourcing means keeping a permanent, ordered list of every change and rebuilding the current state by replaying that list. The supplied code does not do this. It updates job rows in place and saves scan snapshots. The assessment explains that 4,347 source edits measure how often people changed the code. They do not show that any runtime history was lost. It names job ownership and outcome history as the best possible use, and it offers cheaper options such as audit rows written in the same database transaction as the update. Its scores agree with each other and with its "insufficient_evidence" verdict. Two small points were missed, but they do not change the result. First, the repository already rebuilds its saved views from git, which is itself a permanent, ordered record of changes. Second, an imported job-state transition helper suggests that job status changes already go through one shared function.

supporting_evidence_json: The scope lists required interfaces, access by configured targets and MCP profiles, freshness, notes about cut content, distinct CLI and HTTP errors, Retry-After, dry-run, and confirmed restore.
A's control description says no separate scheduling service is proposed, and A's failure note admits there is no crash protection between requests in the shared process.
B's boundary rules say only the gate writes to the store, while B's relationships show the import/export part reading and writing the store.
B lists gate contracts for cooldown wait times. Neither A nor C names an owner for cooldowns.
C's controller contracts define request states, attempt numbers, and restart behavior, and its restore requires stopping the controller.
The design-pattern checks found no repeated designs and no shared shapes.

assessments.change_isolation: A new analysis type reuses the access checks, record saving, and result formatting. A new interface only translates requests and outcomes. The request-handling part takes on every interface's error and output rules, and the proposal admits that this part can grow large.
assessments.control_flow: A handler checks access and then calls one action directly. The action reads inputs, builds findings, and saves a record. The handler then formats the result. Cancellation goes to the running action, which returns an 'interrupted' outcome.
assessments.data_ownership: Access checks own targets, profiles, and service settings. Records own saved findings and their input versions. Setup owns planned changes and restore progress. Handlers keep no state. Setup must go through access checks to change settings, so settings have only one owner.
assessments.decomposition: Five parts: request handling, access checks, analysis, saved records, and setup. Analysis and setup each own a whole action. Access checks and records are kept separate because several actions share them.
assessments.failure_isolation: Each action returns its own outcome. A failed write cannot replace a valid record. Restore checks the backup and the confirmation before it changes anything. A process crash still affects all requests in that process.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers every stated requirement in its rules for each part. Cooldowns and conflict detection are named as outputs but have no clear owner or method. Freshness compares saved input versions with current versions and reports uncertainty when it cannot check. This fits the requirement.
assessments.justified_complexity: This is the least complex proposal. It skips queues and worker processes because the scope asks for no background scheduling. That choice is reasonable, but it is unproven for long or heavy analyses.
assessments.operating_constraints: One installed application with Python 3.11 or newer. It needs no extra service. It does not state limits on workload size. Deployment guidance requires localhost or trusted networks, as the scope demands.
strengths: Each action owns its work, its temporary state, and its outcome from start to finish. Few parts need to coordinate with each other.
The proposal checks access when the request arrives and again on each file read, so the first check is not the only protection.
It is the only proposal that says the saved-record format needs version markers, so readers can spot formats they do not support.
It runs no extra service and no worker processes.
weaknesses: It does not say which part owns cooldown timers or size limits. The 'handled' list includes cooldown errors, but no part decides when a cooldown applies.
It promises to report conflicting changes but gives no method to detect them, such as checking an expected version number before writing.
Cancellation depends on the running code checking for a stop request. Nothing can force-stop an analysis that is stuck.
If analysis crashes the shared process, every request in that process fails. The proposal says it offers no crash protection between requests and cannot resume after a crash.

assessments.change_isolation: New interfaces only call the gate and show the shaped output. New analysis types touch only the engine. Any change to request rules lands in the gate, which concentrates change risk there.
assessments.control_flow: Each request runs once, in a straight line: entry point, gate, then either a store read or snapshot, analysis, and a checked write. After that come the freshness label, cutting to size, and output. Busy targets and cooldowns are refused, not queued.
assessments.data_ownership: The target list owns targets and profiles, and only setup changes them. The store owns all records and never edits them. Setup owns backups. All other parts keep nothing between requests.
assessments.decomposition: The gate, snapshot reader, engine, store, freshness checker, result shaper, entry points, setup, and import/export are separate parts. The analysis engine is a pure function: it takes a file snapshot and returns a record without saving anything.
assessments.failure_isolation: A crash writes nothing, so the last good record stays. Two writers at once cause a conflict error, not a mixed record. A broken import file is rejected before it reaches the store. Restore checks the backup first. There is no protection between requests that share the process.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers access, evidence, freshness, notes about cut content, error kinds, and setup safety. Its handling of interruption is weak, and so are its answers for long analyses. It refuses a second write instead of queuing it, so callers must retry, which the scope allows.
assessments.justified_complexity: There are nine parts, but each one is small and most save nothing between requests. The never-edited records and the expected-pointer write are a cheap way to protect data. Old records are never removed until someone adds a cleanup step.
assessments.operating_constraints: One process with nothing running in the background. It needs Python 3.11 or newer, on localhost or a trusted network. Its cost grows with repository size because of hashing on reads. The proposal itself rates its confidence at 0.6.
strengths: Saved records are never edited. Each target has a pointer to its latest record, and the pointer moves only if the writer names the value it expects. A crash or a second writer cannot leave a half-written result.
It is the only proposal that names one owner, the gate, for cooldown timers, write size limits, and busy-target refusals. It also lists the wait time needed for Retry-After.
Freshness is one comparison of two file hashes made the same way. Every interface labels results identically, and the label says 'unknown' when the repository cannot be read.
Exported records keep their hash, so an imported record is checked for freshness again.
weaknesses: It has no cancellation or interruption path, but the CLI must report an exit code for interruption. Where an interrupted outcome comes from is undefined.
It has no partial results. A crashed analysis saves nothing, so all finished work is lost.
Its own rule says only the gate writes to the store, but import also writes records into the store. That rule and that path disagree.
Hashing the repository files on every read can be slow for large repositories. The proposal admits that caching the hash brings back the risk of stale labels.
The gate holds access, size, cooldown, and concurrency rules and also sends analysis results on to be written. That one part can become hard to change.
The record format has no version marker, so old export files have no stated compatibility rule.

assessments.change_isolation: Adding an analysis type requires defining its inputs, progress units, findings, and failure outcomes. That is more work per type, but the rules are explicit. Output forms read saved records only.
assessments.control_flow: The controller saves an allowed request, copies inputs, and starts a worker attempt. It saves findings as they arrive and decides the final state. After a restart, unfinished work is marked incomplete and resumes only after access and freshness are checked again.
assessments.data_ownership: Only the controller changes request progress and accepts findings. The store owns saved records. Input copying owns the copied files and their hashes. Workers and formatters keep only temporary state.
assessments.decomposition: Entry points, access checks, controller, input copying, workers, record store, result formatting, and setup are separate parts. The controller is the only part that decides whether work is finished.
assessments.failure_isolation: Worker processes contain analysis crashes. A failure while copying inputs stops the analysis from claiming that its inputs are stable. A save failure stops only that request, but a failed store stops all new work. A formatting failure leaves saved results available.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all stated requirements and handles interruption, caller disconnects, and partial work in the most detail. It treats a disconnected caller differently from an explicit cancel. That behavior goes beyond the scope.
assessments.justified_complexity: It is the most complex proposal: saved request states, input copies, a worker pool, attempt numbers, and restart handling. This is justified only if long or crash-prone analyses really happen. The scope gives no workload numbers to confirm that.
assessments.operating_constraints: One installable application with one controller and a limited worker pool. Disk limits and worker limits must come from measured workloads. Operators need to watch queue length, worker failures, and save failures.
strengths: One controller owns each request's progress through clear states: queued, running, then complete, incomplete, failed, or interrupted. Cancellation, restart, and partial results each get a defined meaning.
Analysis runs in separate worker processes, so a crashed or over-budget analysis can be stopped without stopping other requests.
An attempt number rejects late output from a worker that was cancelled or retried.
Inputs are copied before analysis, so evidence points to a fixed set of files. Freshness reports say when the check happened and do not promise anything afterward.
Restore first stops new work and waits for running work to finish.
weaknesses: It does not name an owner for cooldown timers or write size limits.
Copying repository inputs uses disk space and delays the start of each analysis. Worker processes add startup cost.
The single controller and single store are shared failure points and limit how many requests can run at once.
Partial results need each analysis type to define its own units of progress, which adds work for every new type.
It does not define how the record format changes over time.

composition_conflicts: B's records are never edited, while C saves progress updates to its records. Using parts of both requires choosing one way of saving.
B says only the gate writes to the store, but B's import path also writes records into the store. This needs fixing before any of B is reused.
B's rule that only setup writes targets matches A's rule that setup changes settings only through access checks. C does not say how setup changes targets while the controller is running.
C requires all work to stop before a restore. A and B check only the backup, so mixing them leaves open whether restores can overlap with running requests.
disagreements: Refuse or queue: B refuses a second write to the same target and makes the caller retry. C puts requests in a queue state. A does not say.
Cost of protection: A rejects worker processes as unnecessary until workloads are measured. C pays for them up front to contain crashes.
Freshness cost: B accepts hashing the files on every read. C accepts copying inputs to disk. A records input versions without saying how they are computed.

differences: Where rules live: A spreads them across parts that each own a whole action. B gathers access, size, cooldown, and busy-target rules into one gate. C gives request progress and the decision that work is finished to one controller.
Whether records change: B never edits a record and moves a pointer only when the writer names the value it expects. A and C update saved records, and C saves progress and findings together.
Freshness: A compares saved input versions. B hashes the files on every read. C hashes copied inputs and reports when the check happened.
Running analysis: A and B run analysis inside the main process. C runs it in separate worker processes that can be killed.
Interruption: A sends a stop request to the running action. C kills the worker and keeps finished findings. B has no interruption path.
limitations: A and B share the same shape: one process, and each request handled in one pass with nothing in the background. Their differences are in where rules sit and how records are saved, not in how the work runs.
All three use a single local store, and none considers spreading the work across several machines.
No design-pattern checks found repeated designs. Shape comparisons alone cannot prove that two designs mean the same thing.
unexplored_directions: Combining C's input copies with B's never-edited records and expected-pointer writes.
Reusing earlier results for files that have not changed, instead of hashing or copying the whole repository each time.
Making the 'change decisions' part of the purpose concrete, such as previewing the effect of a proposed edit. No proposal does this.
A clear rule for how the saved-record format changes over time, with tests that old files still load.

evidence: The scope lists required interfaces, access by configured targets and MCP profiles, freshness, notes about cut content, distinct CLI and HTTP errors, Retry-After, dry-run, and confirmed restore.
A's control description says no separate scheduling service is proposed, and A's failure note admits there is no crash protection between requests in the shared process.
B's boundary rules say only the gate writes to the store, while B's relationships show the import/export part reading and writing the store.
B lists gate contracts for cooldown wait times. Neither A nor C names an owner for cooldowns.
C's controller contracts define request states, attempt numbers, and restart behavior, and its restore requires stopping the controller.
The design-pattern checks found no repeated designs and no shared shapes.
value_json.summary: All three proposals cover the same required features: shared access checks, results that carry their evidence, freshness labels, notes about what was cut, distinct error kinds, and safe setup. They split the work in different ways. A gives each action, such as analysis or setup, full ownership of its own work, and handlers call these actions directly in one process. B sends every request through one checking gate. It saves results as records that are never edited, and it labels freshness by comparing a hash of the files. C uses a single controller that saves each request's progress, copies repository inputs before analysis starts, and runs the analysis in separate worker processes. A and B both handle a request in one pass in one process. They still differ in where the rules live and in whether records can change after they are saved. C is the only one that handles worker crashes, restarts, and partial results, and it costs the most to run. No proposal is a universal winner.
unknowns: What 'oversized writes' and 'conflicts' refer to: repository changes, saved records, or settings. B reads them as store writes. A and C do not say.
The exact CLI exit codes, size limits, and cooldown rules.
The record format and its compatibility rules across versions.
Real workload sizes, which decide whether C's worker processes or B's per-read hashing are worth their cost.
Whether any proposal was produced in a truly fresh context. All isolation reports are self-reported or unverified.

value_json.summary: The assessment is sound, so I am approving it. It finds no proof that several running copies of AnaxiGraph compete for the same job. It names the two most likely places where one coordinator could matter: scans and graph-cache recovery. It also says that the existing locks may already be enough. Recommending "insufficient_evidence" fits the facts, because the detector found no matching signals and the data on concurrent workers and shared state is missing. Two small points do not justify a revision. First, one placement relies on a single code link to a file whose content was not supplied. Second, the pattern card does not list the whole repository as a target level.

value_json.summary: I agree with the assessment that the evidence is too thin to call AnaxiGraph a Big Ball of Mud. A Big Ball of Mud is a codebase where tangled links make its jobs hard to tell apart or change. The eight sample files show clear jobs, and their main classes hand work to named helper files. design.state_ownership: s08 alone owns saved scans and findings. The bundle exists only during one request. The drafter and checker hold only the current claims. design.summary: Each piece of guidance passes through four steps. Each step changes the data into a new form and owns only that form. First, a bundle builder reads the chosen findings from saved scan results (s08). It gives each finding a short local label and a fingerprint. A fingerprint is a short hash of the finding's content that changes if the content changes. Second, a claim drafter writes claims that cite only those labels. It never reads s08 itself. Third, a citation checker rejects or downgrades any claim whose labels are missing from the bundle. It then swaps each label for a lasting citation made of scan identity, finding identity, and fingerprint. Fourth, when someone inspects the guidance later, a citation opener fetches each cited finding again. It reports whether the finding still matches, has changed, or is missing. Guidance never stores copies of findings. Only s08 owns findings.

value_json.summary: The assessment is sound. A request key is a stable ID that a caller sends again on a retry, so the server can tell a repeat from a new request. The supplied examples show some repeat protection already. Two history-job starts get the same active job ID. Scans reuse snapshots when file fingerprints match. Interrupted graph imports resume from a saved marker. None of the supplied evidence shows a caller-supplied request key, a check that rejects a reused key with different inputs, or a saved reply for a request that already finished. So "insufficient_evidence" is the right call. The scores fit each other: some plausible need, a low demonstrated gap, and low urgency. The proposed places to look are tied to the evidence: the history job service, the forwarded review and agent-submission calls, and the shared store. The assessment also correctly ignores console prints, Git test setup, and browser preference writes as weak hints.

useful_differences: s01: A gives each action its own work and outcome. B gathers request checks in one gate and saves records that never change. Its latest-record pointer moves only if its old value still matches. C saves request progress and runs analysis in separate worker processes. C offers stronger crash recovery at the cost of copied inputs, worker management, and more saved state.

s02: A returns separate pattern and edit judgments. B saves assessments and checks whether a newer scan exists when showing them again. C runs small checks, keeps their separate outcomes, and reports conflicting answers together. A and C leave saving to the parent application. B and C each enforce the rule that advice gives no permission to edit in one place.

s03: A starts a new attempt when resuming. C lets the parent's controller manage attempts and save each result together with its progress. B stores scans as lists of unchanged pieces named by content fingerprints. It continues the same draft and skips equal pieces during comparison. B alone counts storage by category and defines cleanup.

s04: A refuses a next-page request when the saved record version has changed. B keeps built pages for reuse and puts the user's choice in the URL, but has no clear next-page step. C loads views separately and keeps earlier pages when a later page fails. All three reject replies for an older browser choice.

s05: A calculates each output through its own function. C reads evidence once and builds several outputs in one request, with separate completion states. B saves evidence-linked claims and builds outputs from them later. B preserves interpretation history, but questions outside its saved claims may remain unanswered.

s06: A writes advice and checks its citations in the same part. B separates those jobs and later reopens citations to check their fingerprints, which are codes computed from their content. C works item by item and returns finished items after cancellation. B discards partial work on cancellation. A leaves that choice to the parent.

s07: A combines the reuse decision with starting continued analysis. B shares one still-applies check across comparison, continuation, and imports, and separates planning from execution. C lets only the parent controller start work and checks inputs again after planning. That second check catches edits made before execution begins.

s08: A and C send tasks to workers and update saved task records. B adds events to a saved list and rebuilds work status from that list; workers ask for tasks. A and B save incomplete scans. C publishes only after every required task succeeds. B also separates structure reading without AI from AI analysis.

s09: A builds shared statements and formats outputs without a running check. B returns reusable statements and checks that written sentences link to them. That check does not establish matching meaning. C checks sections against cited findings, but its checking method is unproven. C also leaves grouping and design judgments to the parent.

supporting_evidence_json: The s06 scope requires guidance whose supporting evidence the requester can inspect.
The s01 scope requires results to keep evidence, uncertainty, and whether their inputs are still current.
B's design defines a bundle builder, a drafter, a checker, and an opener, and gives each citation a fingerprint.
C's design tracks item states and returns finished items when a request is cancelled.
A's design lists compatibility with parent 2b7c as unconfirmed because of 2b7c's verdict limiter.
The design observations warn that matching shapes or names do not prove that two designs are the same.

assessments.change_isolation: New assessment rules go into the advice writer. That same part also links and checks evidence, so changing the reasoning means working near the citation logic. Only the reader changes when s08 adds a new kind of evidence.
assessments.control_flow: One call reads the findings once, writes the statements with their citations, checks the citations, and returns one result. The parent handles cancellation, saving, and delivery.
assessments.data_ownership: s08 owns the saved findings. The reader and writer keep findings and links only while the call runs. The parent owns any saved assessment.
assessments.decomposition: It has two parts: a reader that fetches the selected findings, and a writer that judges, cites, and checks.
assessments.failure_isolation: If essential findings are missing, the result is marked incomplete and the missing inputs are named. A broken citation removes only the statement that uses it. A process crash loses everything.
assessments.functional_fit: It meets the core need: advice whose evidence the requester can inspect. It also marks unsupported statements as uncertain and lists contrary findings when they are supplied. It does not detect evidence that changes after the advice is saved.
assessments.justified_complexity: This is the smallest of the three designs, and its size fits a direct call. It leaves out separate checking, so it trades some protection for that simplicity.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs in the parent's process. Later inspection works only while s08 still holds the cited findings. Detailed links can make responses longer.
strengths: Each statement gets its supporting findings when it is written. No later step has to guess which findings support finished text.
Each statement has its own links, so a requester can check one recommendation without reading every finding.
It uses only two parts and stores nothing new.
weaknesses: The same part writes the advice and checks its own citations. A mistake in the writer can also weaken the check.
It passes along freshness information only when the parent supplies it. It cannot tell later whether a cited finding changed.
Its fit with parent 2b7c is unconfirmed. That parent's verdict limiter rewrites advice and could break the links between statements and findings.
Cancellation behavior is left to the parent. The payload does not say whether partial work is returned.

assessments.change_isolation: A new kind of assessment changes only the drafting rules. A new kind of evidence changes the bundle builder and the drafter. The checker and opener stay the same.
assessments.control_flow: Bundling, drafting, and checking run in a fixed order on one call. Inspection is a separate later call. That call uses the opener, which reuses the bundle builder. Nothing runs in the background.
assessments.data_ownership: Only s08 owns findings. The bundle lasts for one request. Saved guidance holds scan identity, finding identity, and fingerprint. Match status is recomputed at each inspection and not saved.
assessments.decomposition: It has four steps, each owning one data form: the bundle builder, the claim drafter, the citation checker, and the citation opener for later inspection.
assessments.failure_isolation: If the selected scan is missing, the request stops before any drafting. A bad label downgrades or removes only its claim. Inspection failures change only the status shown, never the saved guidance. A process crash loses the request.
assessments.functional_fit: It meets the core need. It also covers the product-wide requirement to show whether inputs are still current, down to each citation. It is the only design that supports inspection long after the advice was written.
assessments.justified_complexity: The extra steps make sense if saved guidance is inspected later and freshness matters. If guidance is read only right away, the opener and fingerprints add cost with little benefit.
assessments.operating_constraints: Inspection reads s08 again, which can be slow when guidance has many citations. It needs lasting identities for scans and findings. The parent must save extra citation fields.
strengths: The writer sees only a labeled set of selected findings, so it cannot cite evidence that was never selected.
Writing and checking are separate steps. The checker can reject a citation but never add one.
Each citation holds a fingerprint, so a later inspection can say whether the finding still matches, has changed, is missing, or is unknown.
Saved guidance holds citations, not copies of findings. Copies therefore cannot drift away from the original.
All reads from s08 go through one step, so access and missing-data rules apply in one place.
weaknesses: It has four steps and a fingerprint rule. That is the most machinery of the three designs.
The fingerprint rule is undefined. It is unclear whether reworded text should count as a change.
If s08 deletes old scans, citations show as missing.
Cancellation returns nothing, so all partial work is lost.
The fixed step order means a claim cannot ask for more evidence partway through.
Unlike A and C, it does not say that instructions inside the evidence must be treated as data and never followed.

assessments.change_isolation: New assessment questions change only the item writer. A new kind of evidence needs new reference-checking rules. Running items in parallel is postponed until measured delays justify it.
assessments.control_flow: The runner picks questions and handles them one by one. For each one it calls the writer, then the checker, and records the result. It returns one assembled answer.
assessments.data_ownership: The runner holds the item states for one call. The writer and checker keep nothing. s08 or the parent's finding provider keeps the saved findings. The parent owns saved assessments and request attempts.
assessments.decomposition: It has three parts: a request runner that loops over items, an item writer, and an evidence link checker.
assessments.failure_isolation: An error in writing or checking marks only that item as failed. Missing essential input stops the whole request with a stated reason. A process crash loses all temporary work.
assessments.functional_fit: It meets the core need with claim-level support and visible opposing evidence. It handles partial results best of the three. It is weakest at keeping evidence checkable over time.
assessments.justified_complexity: The runner's item states add modest cost. That cost buys partial results and clear per-item outcomes without a separate recovery system.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs in the parent's process. It never fetches newer findings and never widens access. It does not retry failed items automatically.
strengths: Each item has a tracked status: waiting, running, supported, unresolved, failed, or interrupted. One item can fail while earlier items survive.
Cancellation can return finished items instead of nothing.
Writing and checking are separate. Unresolved claims stay visible as questions and are not shown as supported advice.
It says plainly that a valid citation does not prove that the judgment is correct.
weaknesses: Small items can repeat reasoning or give conflicting advice, and the requester must sort that out.
Items run one after another, which can slow broad assessments.
It cannot detect a cited finding that changed after the advice was saved. It relies on freshness information the parent supplies.
Opening the evidence depends entirely on the parent's inspection route and on how long old findings are kept.

composition_conflicts: Parent 2b7c has a verdict limiter that rewrites advice. A and C both send their output through it, and rewriting can break the links between statements and findings. A says its compatibility with 2b7c is unconfirmed.
B requires 2b7c's pin step to be the bundle builder or to feed it. Otherwise two parts would read findings, with two sets of access and missing-data rules.
B's saved guidance needs extra citation fields, such as fingerprints. Each parent must be able to store them.
B notes that the parent designs name s04 as their findings source, while this scope depends on s08. How the two sources relate is unknown.
disagreements: B treats later inspection and change detection as this scope's job. A and C leave both to the parent.
B returns nothing when a request is cancelled. C returns finished items. These are opposite promises to the parent.
A combines judging and checking in one part to avoid guessing citations afterward. B and C keep them separate so the writer cannot approve its own citations.

differences: Who checks citations: in A, the writer checks its own. In B and C, a separate checker does it.
Change detection: only B stores a fingerprint with each citation and rechecks it when someone inspects the guidance. A and C only pass along the freshness information they are given.
Cancellation: C returns finished items. B returns nothing. A leaves it to the parent.
Inspection: B has its own opener step. A and C rely on the parent to open the evidence.
Unit of work: A works per statement within one pass. B works per claim within fixed steps. C works per item, with tracked states.
limitations: A and C differ mainly in C's item loop and its separate checker. Their data ownership and inspection approach are almost the same.
All three run in the parent's process, read findings once, and leave saving to the parent.
None of the three defines how a coding pattern or a proposed change is actually judged.
unexplored_directions: Saving a copy of each cited finding so evidence stays inspectable after s08 deletes old scans.
A second check that tests whether an explanation actually follows from its evidence, beyond checking that the citation exists.
A step that merges or reconciles conflicting advice items.
Letting a claim ask for more evidence partway through a request.

evidence: The s06 scope requires guidance whose supporting evidence the requester can inspect.
The s01 scope requires results to keep evidence, uncertainty, and whether their inputs are still current.
B's design defines a bundle builder, a drafter, a checker, and an opener, and gives each citation a fingerprint.
C's design tracks item states and returns finished items when a request is cancelled.
A's design lists compatibility with parent 2b7c as unconfirmed because of 2b7c's verdict limiter.
The design observations warn that matching shapes or names do not prove that two designs are the same.
value_json.summary: All three designs run inside the parent's call. All three attach each piece of advice to the findings that support it. They differ in four ways: who checks the citations, how much work survives a failure, whether later readers can tell that a cited finding has changed, and who handles opening the evidence. A puts writing and checking in one part. B splits the work into four fixed steps and adds a fingerprint to each citation. A fingerprint is a short code computed from a finding's content, so it changes when the content changes. C builds advice one item at a time and keeps finished items when a later item fails. A and C are close to each other. B is the only design that can later show which cited finding has changed.
unknowns: The rules for judging coding patterns and proposed changes.
Whether s08 keeps old scans, and for how long.
The format of evidence references and how the parent lets requesters open them.
What content the fingerprint should cover in B.
Whether interrupted assessments must be saved.

value_json.summary: The assessment is sound. Two benchmark startup loops retry by catching OSError from a web request. That is the only visible case of an error choosing an ordinary path. Python's urllib has no way to ask "is the server up?" without risking an error, so catching the error is the normal way to write this loop. The other examples reject bad input or report real failures. That is the fail-fast approach (stop at the first sign of a real problem), not this failure mode. "No action" is the right call. The listed issues are small and do not change the result.

value_json.summary: I approve the assessment. Prototype means making a new object by copying a ready-made one instead of building it from scratch. The only example of this in the supplied evidence is execution_for in src/anaxigraph/semantic.py. It uses Python's built-in dataclasses.replace to copy a settings record and change three values. No supplied evidence shows that building any object is slow and repeated with small differences. So "retain" (keep the current approach) and "partial" (the idea appears in one place, not widely) are both fair. The concerns below are small and do not change the recommendation.
